body:
Why Gujarat’s Coast Matters

Gujarat lies on the western coast of India, facing the Arabian Sea. Its coastline is important for international trade, fishing, petroleum and chemical industries, maritime transport and national security. Gujarat also has a sensitive geographical position because its northwestern region of Kutch adjoins Pakistan.

Coastal security means protecting the coast, ports, coastal communities, vessels and nearby maritime areas against unlawful activities and threats. It includes preventing smuggling, unlawful entry and maritime terrorism, while also supporting safe navigation, rescue operations and protection of important installations.

Major Coastal Regions

The Gujarat coast is not a straight line. It contains gulfs, peninsulas, bays, creeks, islands, tidal flats and estuaries. These geographical features are important for both economic activities and security administration.

  • Gulf of Kutch: Located between Kutch and the Saurashtra peninsula. It contains important ports and maritime industrial activities.
  • Saurashtra coast: Includes coastal centres such as Okha, Porbandar and Veraval. Fishing, shipping and coastal settlements are important here.
  • Gulf of Khambhat: Lies between the eastern side of Saurashtra and mainland Gujarat. Rivers such as the Narmada, Tapi, Mahi and Sabarmati reach the Arabian Sea in this broad coastal region.
  • South Gujarat coast: Extends towards the Maharashtra boundary and supports fishing, industries, coastal settlements and maritime transport.
  • Kutch coast and creeks: Includes tidal and marshy environments near the India–Pakistan border, making coordination between maritime and border-security institutions important.

Revised Coastline Length

The length of a coastline depends partly on the scale and method of measurement. A detailed survey records more bends, inlets and other coastal features than a less detailed survey.

On 4 December 2025, the Ministry of Earth Sciences informed Parliament that the National Hydrographic Office, in coordination with the Survey of India, had reassessed India’s coastline using modern geographical information systems and high-resolution high-water-line data. The revised figures had been promulgated through a Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways circular dated 29 April 2025.

AreaEarlier lengthRevised length
Gujarat1,214.70 km2,340.62 km
India7,516.6 km11,098.81 km

Gujarat has the longest coastline among Indian states under the revised figures. The increase is primarily a change in measurement, not a physical extension of the coast. The government also clarified that the revision does not change Coastal Regulation Zone jurisdiction, which is determined through the applicable High Tide Line demarcation.

Ports and Economic Importance

Ports connect maritime trade with inland roads, railways and industrial centres. Gujarat’s location makes it important for trade with West Asia, Africa and other regions connected through the Arabian Sea.

Deendayal Port, historically known as Kandla Port, is a major port in Kutch. Other prominent ports include Mundra and Pipavav. A port’s cargo-handling importance must not be confused with its administrative classification: Deendayal is a major port, while Mundra and Pipavav are non-major ports. Major ports are administered under the central port framework; non-major ports fall under the relevant state framework.

Port security involves several authorities because the risks differ. Port operators manage facilities and access arrangements; police investigate crimes; customs authorities enforce customs laws; and maritime agencies perform their respective security and safety duties. Important industrial sites near the coast also require appropriate protection without interrupting legitimate economic activity.

Coastal Threats and Public Safety

Relevant coastal-security concerns include illegal movement of goods, unauthorized entry, unlawful fishing, maritime terrorism, pollution, vessel accidents and natural disasters. The same stretch of coast can therefore require policing, maritime surveillance, environmental protection and disaster-response coordination.

Fishing communities are important partners in coastal safety because they regularly observe conditions at sea. Registration of fishing vessels, identification documents and communication with authorized agencies help distinguish legitimate activities from incidents requiring attention. Members of the public should report suspicious activity or distress through established authorities rather than attempting an interception themselves.

Prelims focus

  • Gujarat faces the Arabian Sea and has the longest coastline among Indian states.
  • Revised Gujarat coastline: 2,340.62 km; earlier figure: 1,214.70 km.
  • Revised Indian coastline: 11,098.81 km; earlier figure: 7,516.6 km.
  • The revised coastline figures were promulgated on 29 April 2025 and explained to Parliament on 4 December 2025.
  • Deendayal Port, formerly Kandla, is a major port; Mundra and Pipavav are non-major ports.
  • Trap: A revised coastline measurement does not mean that Gujarat physically gained the same amount of coastal land.

[Sources: GCERT Class 9, Social Science, Chapter 13, India: Location, Geological Structure and Physiography—I, printed pp. 99–102; GCERT Class 9, Social Science, Chapter 14, India: Location, Geological Structure and Physiography—II; GCERT Class 10, Social Science, Chapter 14, Transportation, Communication and Trade; Ministry of Earth Sciences, Parliament Question: Coastline of the Country, 4 December 2025, PIB release 2198800; Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Update on Indian Ports Sector up to 31 March 2025. Official coastline data status: 4 December 2025; consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Gujarat’s coast supports fishing, maritime trade and coastal livelihoods.

body:
The Special Geography of the Kutch Border

Gujarat shares an international land boundary with Pakistan in the Kutch region. This border is distinctive because parts of the surrounding landscape consist of salt marshes, tidal creeks and the Rann of Kutch rather than ordinary dry land. The region also connects with the Arabian Sea.

A creek is a relatively narrow water channel or inlet. A tidal creek is influenced by the rise and fall of sea water. Its water level, exposed mudflats and navigable channels can change with the tides. These characteristics make it important to distinguish a boundary on dry land from one associated with a tidal watercourse.

What Is Sir Creek?

Sir Creek is a tidal estuary in the marshy region between Gujarat’s Kutch district and Pakistan’s Sindh province. It is commonly described as approximately 96 km long, although measurements can differ according to the geographical definition used.

The India–Pakistan dispute concerns the alignment of the boundary through the creek. It is not a dispute over the entire Gujarat coastline or the entire Gulf of Kutch.

  • India’s position: The boundary should broadly follow the relevant mid-channel alignment, with reference to the thalweg principle and historical evidence.
  • Pakistan’s position: The boundary should follow the eastern bank of the creek, relying on its interpretation of historical arrangements.

The thalweg principle is a method of delimiting boundaries along a navigable watercourse, generally by reference to its principal navigable channel. Whether that approach applies to Sir Creek, and how historical documents should be interpreted, forms part of the disagreement. The boundary dispute remained unresolved at the 16 November 2026 content cutoff.

Sir Creek is a disputed boundary area. A claimed boundary is not the same as an internationally agreed boundary. The dispute also affects discussions about where the India–Pakistan maritime boundary should begin and how it should extend into the Arabian Sea.

Why Sir Creek Matters

The position of the land boundary’s seaward endpoint affects the delimitation of maritime areas. This can influence competing claims concerning fishing grounds and offshore resources. Fishermen may also face the risk of crossing a disputed or insufficiently clear maritime boundary.

Border security in the Kutch region therefore requires coordination between land-border and maritime authorities. The Border Security Force (BSF), including its Water Wing, has responsibilities related to the international border and creek environment. The Indian Coast Guard performs its maritime duties in the adjoining sea areas. These are distinct institutions with different mandates.

India’s Basic Maritime Zones

Under the Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and Other Maritime Zones Act, 1976, India distinguishes different maritime zones. The following distances are measured from the legally applicable baseline, rather than by adding each zone to the previous one.

Maritime zoneOuter limitBasic legal meaning
Territorial sea12 nautical milesIndia exercises sovereignty, subject to applicable international-law rules such as innocent passage, meaning passage that is not prejudicial to India’s peace, good order or security.
Contiguous zone24 nautical milesIndia may exercise specified preventive and enforcement powers, including on customs, immigration and security matters.
Exclusive Economic Zone200 nautical milesIndia has specified sovereign rights over natural resources and related economic activities, not unrestricted sovereignty over all activities.

A nautical mile equals 1.852 km. The distance limits are general maximums; actual boundaries between neighbouring or opposite states may require delimitation and therefore need not extend to the full theoretical distance.

Applying the Distinctions

A coastal-policing question and a maritime-boundary question may involve the same geographical place but test different concepts. Policing concerns the institution responsible for an activity. Maritime delimitation concerns the legal position of a boundary. Fishing and resource questions may additionally involve rights within the EEZ.

Thus, a claim that India has an EEZ extending up to 200 nautical miles does not mean that every point within that distance is necessarily undisputed or that it is legally identical to India’s territorial sea.

Prelims focus

  • Sir Creek lies between Kutch in Gujarat and Sindh in Pakistan.
  • The dispute concerns the creek boundary and has implications for maritime delimitation.
  • India invokes a mid-channel or thalweg-based interpretation; Pakistan claims an eastern-bank alignment.
  • Territorial sea: 12 nautical miles; contiguous zone: 24 nautical miles; EEZ: up to 200 nautical miles.
  • The BSF has a border-security role in the Kutch creek region; the Coast Guard performs maritime functions.
  • Trap: An EEZ gives important resource-related rights, not complete sovereignty equivalent to the territorial sea.

[Sources: GCERT Class 9, Social Science, Chapter 13, India: Location, Geological Structure and Physiography—I; GCERT Class 11, Geography, Chapter 12, Hydrosphere, printed pp. 87–88; Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and Other Maritime Zones Act, 1976, sections 3, 5 and 7; Indian Express, The Importance of Sir Creek: Why India and Pakistan Have Failed to Solve Border Dispute, October 2025; Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses, The Sir Creek Dispute: Contours, Implications and the Way Ahead. Boundary status checked through sources available by 16 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: From one legal baseline, outer limits are 12, 24 and 200 nautical miles, with distinct sovereignty, enforcement and resource rights.
pictures.caption: Territorial waters, the contiguous zone and the EEZ confer different legal powers.

title: Kutch, Sir Creek and Maritime Boundaries

body:
Why Several Agencies Protect the Coast

Coastal security cannot be assigned to a single organization because the coast links the land, territorial waters, wider maritime areas, ports and international borders. Different agencies possess different legal powers, equipment and responsibilities. Effective coastal security depends on coordination, not on treating all agencies as interchangeable.

India strengthened its maritime-security arrangements after the 26 November 2008 Mumbai terrorist attacks, which demonstrated the seriousness of threats arriving from the sea. An important distinction in the subsequent framework is between overall maritime security, Coast Guard coordination and local coastal policing.

Functions of the Main Agencies

AgencyAdministrative positionPrincipal role in this topic
Indian NavyMinistry of DefenceNational maritime defence and overall maritime-security responsibility.
Indian Coast GuardMinistry of DefenceCoastal-security coordination, maritime law enforcement, surveillance, search and rescue, and protection of maritime interests.
State Marine or Coastal PoliceState police administrationPolicing near the coast, particularly shallow coastal areas, and handling offences within their legal jurisdiction.
Border Security ForceMinistry of Home AffairsGuarding designated international borders, including relevant land and creek sectors in Kutch.
Customs authoritiesCentral customs administrationEnforcing customs law and acting against unlawful movement of goods.
Central Industrial Security ForceMinistry of Home AffairsSecurity of designated ports, installations and other protected facilities.

These responsibilities may overlap in a particular incident. For example, a suspected illegal movement near a fishing harbour may require the coastal police, Coast Guard and customs authorities to exchange information. The involvement of several agencies does not abolish their separate legal mandates.

Indian Coast Guard: Formation and Functions

The Indian Coast Guard (ICG) came into being on 1 February 1977 and was formally inaugurated on 19 August 1978. Its statutory foundation is the Coast Guard Act, 1978. It is an armed force of the Union under the Ministry of Defence, but it is organizationally distinct from the Indian Navy.

Its broad functions include protecting maritime interests, assisting vessels and people in distress, supporting maritime law enforcement, combating smuggling, helping protect the marine environment and coordinating with other authorities on coastal security.

After the 2008 security review, the Indian Navy was designated responsible for overall maritime security, while the Director General of the Indian Coast Guard was designated Commander, Coastal Command, for coordination between central and state agencies on coastal-security matters. This coordinating responsibility does not make the Coast Guard the administrative parent of every coastal police unit.

The Coast Guard’s Gujarat Connection

The Indian Coast Guard Regional Headquarters (North West) was established at Gandhinagar on 16 December 2009. It is responsible for the Coast Guard’s assigned functions in the maritime areas of Gujarat and the adjoining Union Territory region.

Coast Guard activities relevant to Gujarat include maritime surveillance, safety of fishing communities, search and rescue, pollution response and cooperation with the Navy, Marine Police and border authorities. A verified example is the Coast Guard’s rescue of 9 Indian crew members from a vessel in the Arabian Sea on 26 December 2024. The incident illustrates its search-and-rescue function; such assistance is not limited to military operations.

BSF, Marine Police and the Border–Sea Distinction

The BSF is a Central Armed Police Force under the Ministry of Home Affairs. It is not a separate branch of the Army. In Gujarat’s Kutch region, its border responsibilities also relate to the creek environment.

Marine Police, by contrast, form part of the coastal state’s policing arrangements. Their responsibilities include lawful coastal policing, criminal investigation and cooperation with maritime agencies. The Indian Coast Guard is neither the Gujarat Police nor a Central Armed Police Force under the Home Ministry.

Prelims focus

  • Indian Coast Guard established: 1 February 1977; formally inaugurated: 19 August 1978.
  • The Coast Guard operates under the Ministry of Defence.
  • The BSF operates under the Ministry of Home Affairs.
  • The Navy has overall maritime-security responsibility; the Coast Guard coordinates coastal-security agencies.
  • ICG Regional Headquarters (North West) was established at Gandhinagar on 16 December 2009.
  • Trap: Marine Police, BSF, Coast Guard and Navy are not different names for one force.

[Sources: Indian Coast Guard, History, sections on formation and inauguration, consulted 16 November 2026; Ministry of Home Affairs, Measures Taken for Coastal Security, 11 May 2016, PIB release on the three-tier coastal-security arrangement; Ministry of Defence, Defence Secretary Visits Indian Coast Guard Facilities in the North West Region, 2024, PIB release 2016643; Ministry of Defence, Indian Coast Guard Rescues Crew of Nine after Vessel Sinks in Arabian Sea, 26 December 2024, PIB release 2088244; Ministry of Home Affairs, Training of Coastal Police, 17 December 2024, PIB release 2085166.]
